subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Recognition Heuristic
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Recognition Heuristic.

hook.text: Which city is bigger: San Diego or San Antonio? Most Americans guess right by choosing the more familiar name.

buildup.text: Goldstein and Gigerenzer found that recognizing a name is often enough to make accurate judgments.

discovery.text: Recognition heuristic: if you recognize one option but not the other, the recognized one likely ranks higher.

twist.text: Foreign students outperformed Americans on US city size questions by relying purely on recognition.

climax.text: Less knowledge can paradoxically improve accuracy. Recognition carries valid information about importance.

punchline.text: Sometimes knowing less helps you guess better.

quiz.question: Why did foreign students outperform Americans?
options: Recognition alone carried valid information about city size
Americans were confused by too many choices

details.summary: The recognition heuristic makes inferences using a beautifully simple rule: if one of two options is recognized and the other is not, infer that the recognized option has the higher value on the criterion of interest. Recognition alone substitutes for knowledge.
details.whyItMatters: Counter-intuitively, less knowledgeable individuals using recognition can outperform more knowledgeable ones using complex strategies.
takeaways: Recognizing one option but not another provides a valid inferential cue
Less knowledgeable people can outperform experts when recognition is valid
Recognition works because media coverage and cultural prominence correlate with real criteria

faq.question: How can people who know less make better predictions?
faq.answer: American students who recognize some German cities but not others can predict which is larger simply by choosing the recognized one. German students who recognize all cities cannot use this heuristic and must rely on complex but imperfect knowledge.

faq.question: When does the recognition heuristic fail?
faq.answer: When recognition is driven by factors unrelated to the criterion of interest. If a city is recognized only because of a scandal rather than its size, recognition misleads. The heuristic depends on recognition being correlated with the target attribute.
